rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent endpoints and temperature fixed to measure how the crowded central cluster and late pair respond. This comparison will guide subsequent window trimming and temperature adjustments.

Focus the gradient on the observed elution window, retaining a shallow slope while reducing time spent at low organic fraction. The modest slope change also tests whether the remaining close pair can separate without a temperature adjustment.

Keep the promising trimmed gradient and raise temperature to test selectivity for the persistent close pair. Higher temperature should also provide additional time margin for a shallower gradient if needed.
Test an intermediate temperature to retain the central-cluster selectivity gained at 60 C while moving away from the new close pair. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate the temperature effect.

Return to the best temperature and make the gradient shallower to shift the remaining close pair's selectivity. The 7.80-minute last peak at tG 12 leaves room to test this change while targeting elution within 10 minutes.

The close pair appears to cross as the gradient becomes shallower; extend that trend to seek separation on the other side. Raise the starting organic fraction to offset the longer gradient and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with the trimmed gradient, since the higher-temperature region introduces competing close pairs. The 40 C run had only one unresolved pair and enough time margin to test a 10 C decrease.
Test whether cooling further separates the close early-cluster pair seen at 30 C. Shorten the gradient to compensate for increased retention and target a last peak within 10 minutes.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly, from 0.0400 to 0.0375 organic fraction per minute, to improve the sole marginal pair at R 1.40. This small change should preserve the remaining separations while keeping the last peak near but below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is secured; now test a shorter fully resolved run by trimming the low-organic portion of the gradient. Use a shallower slope to help preserve the marginal central pair as the starting organic fraction increases.

Increase the slope modestly from 0.0300 to 0.0333 organic fraction per minute to shorten elution while using the resolution margin from injection 11. Although the programmed gradient is longer, the higher endpoint makes the gradient steeper and should bring the last peak out earlier.

Test further trimming of the low-organic region, with a shallower slope to protect the marginal central pair. This explores whether a higher starting fraction can shorten elution while retaining the maximum CRF.

Explore a faster high-temperature alternative: steepening the gradient may separate the late pair seen in injection 4, while lowering the starting organic fraction helps preserve the early cluster's resolution. Keep the fully resolved 25 C methods as the established benchmark.

Injection 14 is fully resolved in 7.45 minutes but has little resolution margin. Test a small slope increase from 0.0450 to 0.0458 organic fraction per minute to see whether elution can be shortened without losing full resolution.

The fastest fully resolved 60 C method is now bracketed by a slightly steeper method that loses resolution. Explore 35 C with the successful trimmed gradient to test whether intermediate-temperature selectivity offers a faster, more robust alternative to the 25 C methods.

Test a steeper gradient at 35 C to move the crowded central pair away from its current near-coelution while shortening the run. This isolates slope sensitivity in the newly explored temperature region.

Return to 60 C and test a slope between the fully resolved injection 14 and the trimmed-window injection 4. The higher starting fraction may shorten elution, while the intermediate slope tests whether the early cluster and late pair can both retain R ≥ 1.5.

Lower the starting organic fraction to strengthen early-cluster retention, then use a steeper gradient to recover time and separate the later critical pair. This tests whether the fully resolved 7.45-minute result can be shortened without sacrificing resolution.

Test 45 C with a shallower trimmed gradient to seek a fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin than injection 14. This temperature lies between runs showing central-cluster reordering, so the result will check for a useful selectivity window.

Test the shallower side of the late-pair elution-order crossover at 60 C, using the higher starting fraction to limit retention time. This may offer more resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method, which remains injection 14.
Raise the temperature one grid step from fully resolved injection 13 to test a shorter run with the same trimmed gradient. Retain injection 14 as the fastest established method with maximum CRF.

Back off the slope from injection 19 to restore resolution in its two marginal early pairs while retaining separation of the later cluster. This targets another maximum-CRF method near the fastest established operating region.

Test a slightly shallower initial gradient followed by an earlier hold to preserve the early cluster while changing separation of the later critical pair. The fastest established fully resolved method remains injection 14; this endpoint adjustment explores a different local trade-off.

Use the final injection for a small slope reduction from injection 14, targeting more balanced resolution margins around its three near-threshold pairs. The maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 14 remains the fastest established fully resolved method.
